title: Tennis pro mourned after fatal London police shooting
subtitle: A Sarnia tennis pro, who also worked as a massage therapist, has been identified as the man fatally shot by London police in a downtown alley last week.
article: A Sarnia tennis pro, who also worked as a massage therapist, was the man fatally shot by London police in a downtown alley last week, The London Free Press has learned.

Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), says the man involved in the deadly encounter was a 29-year-old Lambton County resident, but the agency hasn't released his name. The president of the Sarnia Tennis Club on Monday identified Justin Bourassa, a longtime club member, competitive player and instructor, as the deceased.
"It's a shock for us," club president Shamel Hosni said.
Bourassa's parents, Jean-Marc and Lorraine, declined through Hosni to speak with the media, but gave him permission to inform the 450-member club of their son's death.
"The emotions are very raw still," he said. "You can imagine what (his) parents are going through right now."

London police responded Thursday about 3:45 a.m. to a reported break-in near St. George and Mill streets. An officer saw a man in a nearby alley on Richmond Row, where there was "an interaction" and an officer shot the man, the SIU said.
One of two police officers involved in the altercation was treated at the hospital for injuries, police said.
Hosni declined to comment on the SIU investigation and said he wasn't aware of who Bourassa was with that night, why he was in London or how often the Sarnia resident went to the Forest City.
"I don't think even his parents know," he said of the details surrounding the investigation. "All the information is a bit sketchy and, given the sensitivity, we don't want to guess about stuff."

The second oldest of four children, Bourassa attended St. Thomas Aquinas elementary school and St. Francois-Xavier secondary school, both French-language schools in Sarnia, where he excelled at all sports, from basketball and tennis to badminton and track and field, childhood friend Scott Donais said.
"He was always a gifted athlete. Basically, whatever sport (he played) he would immediately excel," Donais said. "You name it, he could do it and he was better than anybody else."
Donais, who said he last saw Bourassa one year ago when he came over for drinks with friends, said he doesn't know why his old classmate was in London last week.
The SIU is probing the actions of one officer and has designated 14 officers as witnesses, the agency said.
The watchdog probes all cases of death, serious injuries, allegations of sexual assault and gunfire involving police officers.

It remains unclear whether Bourassa's death - the city's second police-involved shooting this year - is connected to the break-in call that brought London police to the neighbourhood where many Western University students live.

Two women who live in a home at the corner of Mill and St. George streets told The Free Press police showed up at their home around 4 a.m. and told them they were looking for three suspects spotted outside the home with a ladder and tools.

A man seen speaking with a police officer outside the home later Thursday morning told The Free Press he brought a ladder and tools from his nearby home to steal a street sign. The man, who didn't give his name, said he was joined by two other men he didn't know. The man described how he fled after he heard sirens and then the sound of gunfire while he ran away.
The Sarnia Tennis Club is holding a candlelight vigil for Bourassa at 7 p.m. Tuesday.
Bourassa joined the club as a youth, went on to win various titles as a teenager, became the club's head instructor and director of player development and played in international tournaments.
The Lambton College graduate and massage therapist joined the club's board of directors in 2017, but it was as an instructor that he excelled due to his personality, Hosni said.

"I don't recall him ever being angry. I've never seen him as much as frown at anyone. It just wasn't in his nature," he said. "He was quick to smile, quick with humour and people could go to him with all sorts of things to talk about.
"He was just a very gentle soul."
